newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's BHP rocked by management crisis.
newsitem.headline: Australia's BHP rocked by management crisis.

text.p: Australian resources giant, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, (BHP) lost its third senior executive in as many days on Friday, ending three days of management turmoil which wiped about A$2 billion (US$1.5 billion) off its share market value.

News of the latest departure from Australia's biggest listed company came shortly before the close of trading on Friday and sent the group's already shaky stock tumbling, dragging the whole Australian share market to a lower close.
BHP told the market the latest executive to quit, petroleum division chief, John O'Connor, had irreconcilable differences with the board.
The resignation compounded market uncertainty after the sudden departures of minerals division chief Dick Carter and iron ore head Geoff Wedlock over the previous two days.

BHP managing director, John Prescott and chairman, Jerry Ellis later told a hastily convened briefing that O'Connors exit was the result of a long-term disagreement with the board about floating-off the petroleum unit, BHP's biggest earner.
O'Connor was reported in some newspapers this week as having promoted the float option during briefings with analysts in Sydney and Melbourne.
"The recent events were the straw that broke the camel's back, that's the reason for the timing in respect of Mr O'Connor," Ellis said.
Both Ellis and Prescott said the board had discussed the possibility of a float for a long period and several months ago had decided unanimously against the proposal.
BHP's Prescott said while the three resignations had a 'regrettable coincidence', they were essentially unrelated.
Asked about Carter's departure, Prescott said it came at the same time BHP announced there had been cost overuns at its Pilbara hot briquetted iron (HBI) project in Western Australia.
"The concern there was not so much the inability to arrive at a final figure for that project but whether we had the processes for managing that project fully under control," he said.
The HBI plant was originally expected to cost A$1.2 billion but was most recently pegged at A$1.65 billion. Analysts speculate the latest cost blow-out could be up to 10 percent.
BHP closed 45 cents lower at A$16.99 and the All Ordinaries index, which looked as if it would close fairly steady, lost 9.4 points to 2,717.7.
The steel, oil and mining giant now has a capitalisation of A$34 billion.
Analysts said the senior management turmoil would continue to be negative for BHP's shares in the short term.
"I'm sure it it will take a hit here and overseas tonight, but the underlying assets are good and some people will see it providing ample opportunity to buy," said one BHP analyst.
BHP analyst at broker HSBC James Capel, Umit Safak, said he expected the company's share price to track lower in the short term but viewed a prolonged fall as a good buying opportunity.

"Everything is not rosy at the top. There are some major differences of opinion and cracks within management and they are definitely wider than hairline cracks, but I don't think we are looking at the Grand Canyon either," Safak said.
Prescott said the board would look first within BHP for replacements for the three senior executive and said the company had considerable talent within its ranks to fill the positions.
